Upgrading from DesignLibrary 0.1: what changes, what does not, and why

Source: vignettes/upgrading.Rmd
upgrading.Rmd

The short version

DesignLibrary 2.0 replaces the designer functions of 0.1 with a library of self-contained design files, read through make_design(). It requires DeclareDesign, fabricatr, estimatr, and randomizr 2.0.

All fifteen 0.1 designers keep their names and their argument names, with two exceptions: block_cluster_two_arm_designer() loses six arguments, and three arguments (label_E1 and label_E2 of process_tracing_designer(), and args_to_fix of every designer) are accepted but ignored with a warning. Each now builds a library design, so two_arm_designer(N = 40) returns the same design as make_design("two_arm_flexible", N = 40). Most 0.1 scripts that call a designer and diagnose the result run unchanged.

There are two types of break:

  • Removed functions and removed arguments stop with an error that names the replacement.

  • A handful of changes do not error. These aries if there is a changed default, renamed inquiries, or renamed estimator terms or different step names. See Porting an existing script for more.

What does not change

A 0.1 script like this one runs as written. As in 0.1, library(DesignLibrary) also attaches DeclareDesign, fabricatr, estimatr, and randomizr.

library(DesignLibrary)

design <- two_arm_designer(N = 100, ate = 0.25)
set.seed(343)
draw_estimates(design)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 12
#>   term  estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high    df outcome
#>   <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1 Z      -0.0159     0.171   -0.0929   0.926   -0.356     0.324    98 Y      
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: estimator <chr>, inquiry <chr>, estimand <dbl>

What carries over:

  • The fifteen designer names: two_arm_designer(), two_arm_attrition_designer(), two_arm_covariate_designer(), pretest_posttest_designer(), randomized_response_designer(), mediation_analysis_designer(), multi_arm_designer(), two_by_two_designer(), factorial_designer(), block_cluster_two_arm_designer(), regression_discontinuity_designer(), spillover_designer(), cluster_sampling_designer(), binary_iv_designer(), and process_tracing_designer().
  • Their argument names and defaults, except for block_cluster_two_arm_designer() and the default N of multi_arm_designer().
  • Inquiry and estimator labels, except for the cases listed below.
  • The designs themselves. Seven of the designers became new library files (two_arm_covariate, regression_discontinuity_polynomial, spillover, cluster_sampling, binary_iv, process_tracing_bayes, and factorial) flattened from their 0.1 code, and at the same arguments and seed each draws what its 0.1 designer drew.

What changes, and why

Removed functions

Four aliases that 0.1 had already deprecated are gone, along with two helpers. In each case you get an informative message.

simple_two_arm_designer(N = 50)
#> Error in `.defunct_01()` at DesignLibrary/R/defunct.R:30:3:
#> ! `simple_two_arm_designer()` was removed in DesignLibrary 2.0.0.
#> ℹ Use `two_arm_designer()`, which takes the same arguments.
Removed Use instead
simple_two_arm_designer() two_arm_designer(), same arguments
simple_factorial_designer() two_by_two_designer(), same arguments
simple_iv_designer() binary_iv_designer(), same arguments
simple_spillover_designer() spillover_designer(), same arguments
get_design_code() get_code("<id>")
match.call.defaults() match.call() and formals()

In 0.1 every designer pasted its own source code into an attribute of the design it returned, and get_design_code() read that attribute back. In 2.0 the source of a design is a file in the package, so there is nothing to paste: get_code() prints the file. Each designer’s help page names the id of the file it builds.

get_design_code(two_arm_designer())
#> Error in `.defunct_01()` at DesignLibrary/R/defunct.R:65:3:
#> ! `get_design_code()` was removed in DesignLibrary 2.0.0.
#> ℹ Designs no longer carry their code as an attribute.
#> ℹ Use `get_code()` with a library design id, for example `get_code("two_arm_flexible")`.
#> ℹ `list_designs()` lists the ids, and each designer's help page names the id it builds.
get_code("two_arm_flexible")
#> design <-
#>   declare_parameters(
#>     N = 100,
#>     assignment_prob = 0.5,
#>     control_mean = 0,
#>     control_sd = 1,
#>     ate = 1,
#>     treatment_sd = 1,
#>     rho = 1
#>   ) +
#>   declare_model(
#>     N = N,
#>     u_0 = rnorm(N),
#>     u_1 = rnorm(n = N, mean = rho * u_0, sd = sqrt(pmax(0, 1 - rho^2))),
#>     potential_outcomes(
#>       Y ~ control_mean +
#>           (1 - Z) * (u_0 * control_sd) + Z* (u_1 * treatment_sd + ate)
#>     )
#>   ) +
#>   declare_inquiry(ATE = mean(Y_Z_1 - Y_Z_0)) +
#>   declare_assignment(Z = complete_ra(N, prob = assignment_prob)) +
#>   declare_measurement(Y = reveal_outcomes(Y ~ Z)) +
#>   declare_estimator(Y ~ Z, inquiry = "ATE")

The description, definitions, and shiny_arguments attributes went with code. Now get_args() and design_info() describe a design’s parameters.

block_cluster_two_arm_designer() takes new arguments

The 0.1 designer derived its level sizes from N and its three shock standard deviations from one total sd, through defaults that referred to each other. Its defaults also produced a design with no blocking and no clustering (one block of 100 single-unit clusters) and no effect. The 2.0 designer takes the level sizes and the shocks directly, and its defaults are a blocked and clustered design with an effect to find: 20 blocks of 4 clusters of 10 units, each shock with standard deviation 0.577, and ate = 0.2.

The 0.1 arguments N, sd, sd_i_1, rho, control_mean, and treatment_mean are errors that say what to set instead.

block_cluster_two_arm_designer(N = 200, rho = 0.5)
#> Error in `block_cluster_two_arm_designer()`:
#> ! `block_cluster_two_arm_designer()` no longer takes `N`, `rho` (DesignLibrary 0.1).
#> ℹ Set the sample size through `N_blocks`, `N_clusters_in_block`, and `N_i_in_cluster`.
#> ℹ Treatment and control potential outcomes are perfectly correlated; `rho` is not supported.
design <- block_cluster_two_arm_designer(
  N_blocks = 5, N_clusters_in_block = 4, N_i_in_cluster = 10, ate = 0.1
)

assignment_probs takes one probability rather than one per block, and verbose is ignored with a warning. Because the defaults changed, block_cluster_two_arm_designer() with no arguments is a different design in 2.0, and nothing warns about it.

multi_arm_designer() has a larger default sample

As in 0.1, the designer declares an inquiry for every pair of arms and estimates each by a difference in means between its two arms, under labels like "DIM (Z_2 - Z_1)". The default N went from 30 to 90, so that each of the three arms has 30 units rather than 10.

design <- multi_arm_designer(m_arms = 3)
set.seed(343)
draw_estimates(design)[, c("estimator", "term", "estimate", "inquiry")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   estimator       term  estimate inquiry  
#>   <chr>           <chr>    <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1 DIM (Z_2 - Z_1) Z2      -0.621 ate_Y_2_1
#> 2 DIM (Z_3 - Z_1) Z3      -0.350 ate_Y_3_1
#> 3 DIM (Z_3 - Z_2) Z3       0.271 ate_Y_3_2

Two renamings that change no values

mediation_analysis_designer()’s inquiries Indirect_0 and Indirect_1 are now Mediator_Effect_0 and Mediator_Effect_1. Each is the effect of the mediator on the outcome with treatment held at 0 or at 1.

draw_estimands(mediation_analysis_designer())
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   inquiry             estimand
#>   <chr>                  <dbl>
#> 1 FirstStage             0.335
#> 2 Mediator_Effect_0      0.4  
#> 3 Mediator_Effect_1      0.4  
#> 4 Controlled_Direct_0    0.5  
#> 5 Controlled_Direct_1    0.5  
#> 6 Natural_Direct_0       0.5  
#> 7 Natural_Direct_1       0.5

process_tracing_designer() fixes its estimator labels at "Straw in the Wind" and "Smoking Gun".

design <- process_tracing_designer(label_E1 = "Hoop")
#> Warning: label_E1 and label_E2 are ignored; the estimator labels are fixed.

args_to_fix is ignored

0.1 designers could fix arguments into the returned design so that expand_design() could not vary them. In 2.0 every parameter stays redesignable on the design object, and a non-empty args_to_fix warns.

design <- two_arm_designer(args_to_fix = "N")
#> Warning: args_to_fix is ignored; parameters remain redesignable on the design
#> object.

Designs are now all DeclareDesign 2.0 designs

DeclareDesign 2.0 has no separate potential outcomes or reveal steps: potential outcomes live in declare_model() and are revealed in declare_measurement(). Some step names differ as a result. factorial_designer()’s inquiry step, for example, was "ATE" and is now "inquiry".

names(factorial_designer())
#> [1] "parameters"  "model"       "assignment"  "measurement" "inquiry"    
#> [6] "estimator"

Inquiry and estimator labels are otherwise those of 0.1. Code that picks a step by name or by position (design[[3]]) needs checking, since the position of a step can change even where its name does not.

Sweeping a parameter

expand_design() still works but is deprecated in DeclareDesign 2.0. Pass a vector to redesign() instead, which needs no designer function at all.

designs <- redesign(two_arm_designer(), N = c(50, 100))
length(designs)
#> [1] 2

One caution: process_tracing_designer() checks that cor_E1E2_H and cor_E1E2_not_H are compatible with the clue probabilities, and redesign() does not. An incompatible value passed through redesign() fails only when the design is run, with “negative probability” from the measurement step.

The rows in bold are the ones to search for deliberately, since nothing will point you to them.

What is new

A library of simple design files sit at the heart of library 2.0. The library holds 75 designs, including the declarations from Research Design in the Social Sciences.

  • list_designs() browses the library
  • make_design() builds a design and changes its parameters
  • get_args() lists what can be changed
  • get_code() prints the source
  • run_shiny() opens thelibrary in a browser
  • vignette("DesignLibrary") gives you a tour.
